Welcome to #beginners: this topic exists specifically so you don't have to feel like you need a PhD to ask a question.

Whether you're just discovering formal verification, trying to understand what BAIF actually does, or wondering what any of the acronyms in this channel mean, this is the right place. No question is too basic. The only rule is that everyone here was a beginner once, and we treat it that way.

A few questions to get you started if you're not sure what to ask:

  • What brought you to the AI safety / formal verification space?
  • Is there a concept you keep seeing but haven't fully wrapped your head around yet?
  • What would make this community most useful for you as you're getting started?

Jump in :point_up:
Is there well known list of bite sized problems to implement and prove, or just prove? so you don't have to think about this things when you just learning the ropes

Will there a mechanism to claim and work on tasks for a reasonable length of time? I don't know if it makes sense for me or anyone else to work on tasks where someone or an AI might just scoop it up and finish it.

I'll try to release my work in the coming days.
Looking at: https://www.beneficialaifoundation.org/blog/signal-shot
I believe the main open problems are proving (in Aeneas) that the production code is equivalent to the Hax reference implementation.

For now, you can look at existing functional correctness proofs for the curve25519-dalek Rust crate for cryptographic algorithms.

https://github.com/Beneficial-AI-Foundation/curve25519-dalek-lean-verify

See for instance the specs in

https://github.com/Beneficial-AI-Foundation/curve25519-dalek-lean-verify/tree/master/Curve25519Dalek/Specs/Backend/Serial/U64/Scalar/Scalar52

We are still preparing some repos where you can try verifying the functional correctness of some Rust implementations in the Signal app. See for instance:

https://github.com/Beneficial-AI-Foundation/libsignal-verify

https://github.com/Beneficial-AI-Foundation/sparsepostquantumratchet-verify

For want of a new topic, may I ask what the concrete verification goals are? What model do we use for formalizing, say, adversaries, hard problems and reductions.? What sort of theorems do we prove at the top level? Is it Dolev Yao style equational verification?
I would also appreciate clarification on this!

Bas Spitters said:

I'll try to release my work in the coming days.
Looking at: https://www.beneficialaifoundation.org/blog/signal-shot
I believe the main open problems are proving (in Aeneas) that the production code is equivalent to the Hax reference implementation.

Here's one precise question: Can we prove (in Aeneas?) that rust reference implementations are equivalent to the "HACSpec" reference implementations.
Here are some examples:
https://github.com/spitters/libcrux-lean-specs
In a way this is backwards, as most of these are already formally verified (in F*), but we need some way to connect production code with clean mathematical models we can use in Lean

Thanks @Shreyas Srinivas and @Nadim Kobeissi for your questions. At BAIF, we are thinking carefully about the best path forward and should have more information soon. There are some details about how we are staging Signal Shot in our blog post: https://www.beneficialaifoundation.org/blog/signal-shot

In short, we want to deliberate carefully what the spec-theorems (what we are trying to prove about the models of protocols) should be (Stage 1A). This then leads to the specifications that we want to verify against the Rust implementations. The specifications will likely involve the Rust reference implementations that @Bas Spitters mentioned.

Some of the Rust implementations will have obvious specifications. We are trying to get those out first (Stage 1B) in parallel to deliberation on the spec-theorems (Stage 1A). We want to make sure that all of this is done in a way that improves tooling for software verification beyond Signal Shot. For example, a single AI-generated PR with proposed spec-theorems and proofs will almost definitely be rejected because it makes careful human review of the specs and tools difficult. Thank you for your patience as we navigate this as a community :blush:
Devon Tuma (VCV-io) shared this very cool tutorial on FV of cryptographic primitives and protocols: https://proof-ladders.github.io/
Is there space for AI contributions? If there are some unfilled sorrys, I'd love to try to get my Claude to fill them and make PRs! Is that welcome?

Hi @Vasily Ilin ! Thanks for the interest! We currently have contributing MD files where there's relevant info you might want to look at! In general, we're trying for now to make PRs without sorry's as far as possible (it's easier to audit in a review), so I'm not sure how many are present and if they are it might also be that it's WIP the same author is wrapping up.

Do you have any target in mind? it's always good to connect/coordinate with the code owners of the repos and I can help get you in touch with them :)

I just like to try Claude's hand at different formalizations, out of curiosity, as a kind of personal ever-moving benchmark. Of course, the biggest obstacle is that when I let it make new definitions and statements, they usually come out not idiomatic and too narrow. That's why I asked about unfilled holes

yes, the spec part is tricky and usually you need to carefully guide LLMs towards something sensible. The proof part is getting better, the proof might be ugly, but they manage to close it most of the times
